lines: Jamie Alvarez
+1 (555) 010-5820 | jamie.alvarez@example.com | example.com/in/jalvarez
EDUCATION
Riverbend Polytechnic | B.S. in Industrial Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2014 - May 2018
EXPERIENCE
Greenleaf Florist | Delivery Driver and Shop Assistant | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Delivered 30 to 40 arrangements a day across the city and took cash and card payments at the door.
- Prepared weekend wedding orders with the head florist and kept the cooler stocked and labeled.
Lakeview Distribution | Operations Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2018 - Jan 2021
- Raised forecast accuracy from 70% to 85% by switching the MAPE calculation to cover only SKUs that sold every week.
- Ran a time study of the returns desk; my findings led to a triage station that cut returns processing time from 3 days to 1.
- Wrote the dock scheduling rules for 12 carriers, cutting average trailer wait at the dock from 95 to 40 minutes.
- Set up cycle counting for the 2,000 highest-value locations, raising inventory record accuracy from 91% to 98.5% within a year.
Crestway Foods | Supply Chain Planner | Metro City, USA | Feb 2021 - Jul 2025
- Rebuilt weekly demand planning for 1,400 SKUs across 3 distribution centers with a seasonal forecast model, cutting stockouts from 6.2% to 2.8% while inventory fell by $1.9M.
- Cut inbound freight cost per pallet from $48 to $41 over two quarters by consolidating supplier pickups into four regional milk runs.
- Set reorder points for every SKU from 18 months of daily demand and supplier lead-time data, reviewed monthly with the category managers.

- Scoring 40 vendors weekly on on-time delivery, fill rate, lead-time variance and invoice accuracy, and sharing the scorecards with buyers before each quarterly review, raised on-time inbound deliveries from 81% to 93%.
- Raised the packaging line's overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) from 71% to 112% by cutting changeover time and micro-stops.
- Trained 6 planners on the new forecasting workflow and wrote its exception-handling guide, which the team still uses for promotions.
PROJECTS
Last-Mile Routing Study | Independent Project | Python | Oct 2024 - Present
- Modeled a regional grocer's 85 daily delivery stops as a vehicle-routing problem, cutting planned route miles 18% against the grocer's current routes.
- Cut average route length from 120 to 90 miles, a 40% reduction, by solving the routing problem with customer time windows.
- Raised on-time deliveries by 9% in simulation, from 84% to 93%, by adding customer time windows to the routing model.
Regional Food Bank Warehouse | Volunteer Consultant, Team of 4 | Excel | Mar 2022 - Jul 2022
- Analyzed warehouse operations and made recommendations to the food bank's leadership.
- The donation intake process was mapped and two duplicate data-entry steps were removed, so donations reached the shelves a day sooner.
- Wrote a slotting guide that the volunteer coordinators used to re-slot the warehouse again after its spring expansion.
SKILLS
Tools: Excel, Python
Methods: demand forecasting, inventory planning, time studies, vehicle routing

items.says: Verify the profile URL and use a live professional link.
items.because: It looks like placeholder text, and the displayed link should match its destination.

items.says: Consider adding a city and state.
items.because: Location can help recruiters determine eligibility and fit for location-specific roles.

items.says: Add strong, relevant academic details if useful.
items.because: GPA, honors, scholarships, or coursework may strengthen the candidacy, though work experience matters more for a 2018 degree.

items.says: Make the education entry’s separators and formatting consistent with other entries.
items.because: Institution, degree, location, and dates should receive the same treatment throughout.

items.says: Consider omitting the education location if space is needed.
items.because: That space may be more useful for a summary, certifications, or relevant skills.

items.says: Verify that the current role’s “Present” date is accurate.
items.because: The résumé needs to be recent enough to support that designation.

items.says: Reconsider how prominently the florist role appears.
items.because: It is substantially less related to supply-chain analytics than the prior work.

items.says: Clarify what the 30-to-40-arrangement volume represents.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether it is a daily average, range, or peak-day volume.

items.says: Add a performance or responsibility outcome.
items.because: The bullet reads as a basic job description without evidence of quality, reliability, or delivery performance.

items.says: Clarify the payment responsibility if material.
items.because: Reconciliation, transaction accuracy, or cash control would make it more relevant to operations.

items.says: Fix any wrapping that strands “at the.”
items.because: The visual issue affects polish.

items.says: Quantify the scale of wedding-order preparation.
items.because: Volume, event size, or deadline pressure would show the work’s scope.

items.says: Clarify your ownership of the wedding-order work.
items.because: “With the head florist” sounds supportive without identifying your responsibilities.

items.says: Make the cooler inventory work more operationally specific.
items.because: “Stocked and labeled” is basic without a result such as fewer errors or better stock rotation.

items.says: Consider whether the florist role needs two bullets.
items.because: Space may be better preserved for more relevant experience.

items.says: Explain why the MAPE population changed and whether the figures are comparable.
items.because: Excluding SKUs that did not sell every week can make the metric appear better without improving the forecast.

items.says: Clarify how “forecast accuracy” was derived from MAPE.
items.because: MAPE is an error metric, so calling it accuracy can confuse technically informed readers.

items.says: Add the operational consequence of the forecast work if available.
items.because: The bullet does not connect the measurement or process to inventory, service, labor, or planning decisions.

items.says: Remove “my findings.”
items.because: First-person phrasing is inconsistent with the other action-oriented bullets.

items.says: Define the returns processing-time measure.
items.because: It is unclear whether the figures are calendar days, business days, or average queue-to-completion time.

items.says: Explain your contribution to implementing the triage station.
items.because: The bullet does not show whether you designed the workflow, supported implementation, or measured the result.

items.says: Check whether the semicolon structure is easy to scan.
items.because: The bullet contains two substantial ideas that may need clearer separation.

items.says: Clarify what the dock scheduling rules covered.
items.because: The scheduling mechanism could involve appointment windows, priority, carriers, or dock assignments.

items.says: Explain how the rules were implemented.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether they were adopted, embedded in a system, or used manually.

items.says: Define the trailer-wait measurement basis.
items.because: The average could cover all trailers, a carrier group, or a selected period.

items.says: Clarify what “locations” means.
items.because: Readers may interpret it as storage locations, SKUs, or inventory positions.

items.says: Add the cycle-counting design if relevant.
items.because: Frequency, priority, or escalation rules would strengthen the bullet.

items.says: Specify how inventory record accuracy was measured.
items.because: The result could come from audit variance, system-to-physical comparison, or another measure.

items.says: Define the $1.9M inventory reduction and its measurement period.
items.because: It could refer to average inventory, ending inventory, working capital, or inventory value, and its sustainability is unclear.

items.says: Define the stockout metric’s denominator.
items.because: It could refer to SKU-location stockouts, order lines, customer orders, or something else.

items.says: Add the improvement time frame.
items.because: Readers cannot tell how long the change took or whether the comparison is year-over-year or before-and-after.

items.says: Make the seasonal-model claim supportable with method or validation detail.
items.because: The forecasting method, system, or validation process is not identified.

items.says: Put the per-pallet saving in broader business context.
items.because: Recruiters may want to know the total or annualized savings.

items.says: Explain your role in designing the milk runs.
items.because: The bullet does not distinguish analysis, route design, carrier coordination, negotiation, or monitoring.

items.says: Verify that the baseline and final periods are comparable.
items.because: “Over two quarters” does not establish how each cost was measured.

items.says: Add an outcome for the reorder-point work.
items.because: The bullet describes responsibility without showing an effect on service, inventory, workload, or stockouts.

items.says: Clarify the scope of “every SKU.”
items.because: Absolute wording invites questions if it meant only a category or network.

items.says: State the reorder-point method if relevant.
items.because: Safety stock, variability, service targets, or order constraints would strengthen technical credibility.

items.says: The opening “Scoring” makes the bullet a sentence fragment.
items.because: It is inconsistent with the past-tense style of the other experience bullets.

items.says: Clarify how the scorecards produced the delivery improvement.
items.because: The wording implies direct causation without explaining corrective actions or supplier management.

items.says: Resolve when buyers received the scorecards.
items.because: Weekly scoring and sharing before quarterly reviews leave the timing ambiguous.

items.says: Use consistent list punctuation.
items.because: The final list item lacks a comma if the résumé uses the Oxford comma.

items.says: Clarify the scope of the 40 vendors.
items.because: Whether they were all strategic suppliers or a category would add context.

items.says: An OEE value of 112% is generally invalid.
items.because: Overall equipment effectiveness is normally between 0% and 100%, so the figure suggests a calculation or terminology error.

items.says: Quantify the changeover and micro-stop improvements.
items.because: Their reductions or effects on availability, performance, and quality would explain the claimed result.

items.says: Clarify your role and the packaging-line project’s scope.
items.because: The bullet does not show whether you analyzed, led, implemented, or coordinated the work.

items.says: Clarify the scope of training six planners.
items.because: It is unclear whether they represented one site, one team, or the full planning organization.

items.says: Clarify “still uses.”
items.because: The phrase is informal and does not explain how the guide was adopted or what problem it solved.

items.says: Add a measurable training or workflow result if available.
items.because: The bullet does not show an effect on planning cycles, overrides, consistency, or errors.

items.says: Clarify the independent project’s data source and status.
items.because: Its reference to a grocer’s current routes does not show whether the data was real, public, anonymized, or constructed.

items.says: Define “planned route miles.”
items.because: It could mean total fleet miles, average route miles, or miles per day.

items.says: Reconcile the 18% reduction with the next bullet’s reduction.
items.because: The claims cannot describe the same comparison unless they use different baselines.

items.says: Clarify whether the route result was simulated or implemented.
items.because: An independent project should not imply the grocer adopted the routes unless it did.

items.says: The stated 40% reduction from 120 to 90 miles is incorrect.
items.because: A 30-mile reduction from 120 miles is 25%.

items.says: Clarify the average-route baseline and sample.
items.because: Readers need to know how many routes, vehicles, or days the comparison includes.

items.says: Avoid attributing the entire route-length reduction to time windows without a test.
items.because: The causal claim is too strong unless models with and without time windows were compared.

items.says: Describe the solver or routing approach if relevant.
items.because: “Python” does not show whether the project used a library, heuristic, or custom algorithm.

items.says: Define “on-time.”
items.because: It could mean within a customer window, before a deadline, or within a tolerance.

items.says: Explain the 84% baseline and comparison design.
items.because: It is unclear whether other model settings remained constant.

items.says: Distinguish the effects of route optimization from adding time windows.
items.because: Multiple major improvements across the project bullets are attributed to time windows.

items.says: Reduce overlap among the routing outcome bullets and show more technical process.
items.because: The bullets give several outcomes but too little on data preparation, formulation, constraints, testing, or validation.

items.says: Replace the generic warehouse summary with the actual scope of work.
items.because: It does not show what was analyzed, which methods were used, or what changed.

items.says: Clarify your individual role on the four-person team.
items.because: The heading gives team size but not your contribution.

items.says: Use a direct action-bullet structure.
items.because: The passive narrative differs from most other bullets.

items.says: Clarify your contribution to the intake change.
items.because: It does not show whether you mapped the process, found the duplication, or supported implementation.

items.says: Define the one-day improvement.
items.because: It could be average processing time, elapsed time, or arrival-to-shelf time.

items.says: Clarify whether the change was implemented or only recommended.
items.because: This bullet suggests implementation while the first project bullet says recommendations were made.

items.says: Remove the redundant “re-slot” and “again” wording.
items.because: The two expressions repeat the same idea.

items.says: Quantify the slotting guide’s scope and result if available.
items.because: The number of zones, categories, locations, or volunteers affected is not shown.

items.says: Explain why the slotting guide mattered.
items.because: Its effect on travel, space, replenishment, accessibility, or consistency is not stated.

items.says: Clarify the expansion timeline.
items.because: The chronology of writing and using the guide should be easy to understand.

items.says: Add proficiency-relevant details for Excel and Python.
items.because: The tool names alone are broad and do not show capabilities.

items.says: List relevant libraries or advanced Excel features if applicable.
items.because: Specific tools used in routing, forecasting, or analysis would be more informative.

items.says: Consider adding operational systems used.
items.because: ERP, WMS, TMS, planning, SQL, or BI systems may be more valuable than a short generic list.

items.says: Add relevant methods demonstrated elsewhere in the résumé.
items.because: The experience also shows supplier management, cycle counting, scheduling, process mapping, slotting, milk-run design, and OEE analysis.

items.says: Keep skills capitalization consistent.
items.because: Sentence case or title case should be applied throughout.

items.says: Support the strongest listed skills with evidence in the bullets.
items.because: A skills list should not compensate for missing experience or project evidence.

items.says: Consider adding a certification section if you hold relevant credentials.
items.because: Lean Six Sigma, APICS/ASCM, or analytics certifications could strengthen the résumé.

items.says: Check wrapped lines and page layout, including awkward short fragments.
items.because: Manual line breaks can also damage ATS parsing.

items.says: Consider adding a short professional summary.
items.because: It could connect the industrial engineering and supply-chain background, contextualize the florist role, and signal the target position.
